one_liner: Single-header C hash table beating std::unordered_map on lookups, erasures, and iteration; insertion only average.
what_it_does: Verstable is a generic, type-safe hash map/set for C, instantiated via macro templates (#define NAME/KEY_TY/[VAL_TY] then #include "verstable.h"), producing a distinct struct and a set of NAME_-prefixed functions (or C11 generic vt_* macros) per instantiation. It is not a drop-in std::unordered_map replacement — different types, function-call API, and manual cleanup — but is callable from C++ by wrapping the include in extern "C". It targets the speed and memory efficiency of state-of-the-art C++ tables (Abseil/Swiss, Boost, Bytell) inside plain C.
how_it_is_fast: It's open addressing with quadratic probing, but colliding keys that hash to the same 'home bucket' are linked into a chain via an 11-bit displacement value; a 1-bit flag keeps each chain rooted at its home bucket by evicting non-belonging occupants on insert. This chain metadata, plus a 4-bit hash-code fragment per bucket, lives in a separate uint16_t array instead of alongside the key/value, so lookups can skip most non-matching keys without touching the buckets array or calling the comparison function, and iteration walks a compact metadata array rather than sparse, cache-missing buckets. Deletion and insertion move at most one existing key and require no tombstones. The author describes it as a hybrid of open addressing and separate chaining, related to Malte Skarupke's Bytell table and classic coalesced hashing.
when_to_use: C code that needs a generic, type-safe hash map/set without hand-rolling one, or C++ code that can call a C API via extern "C"
Lookup- and iteration-heavy workloads, including lookups of nonexisting keys, where std::unordered_map's node-based layout causes cache misses
Large keys/values or expensive hash/compare functions, since insert/delete move at most one existing key instead of shifting many (unlike Robin Hood schemes)
High load factors, since the design is described as largely impervious to load factor for lookup speed
Willing to vendor a single header and accept a non-STL API in exchange for speed
when_not_to_use: Need a true drop-in std::unordered_map replacement with C++ container semantics, allocator/exception conventions, or STL iterator guarantees
Insertion throughput is the dominant cost: the benchmark author calls Verstable's insertion 'only average', and it sits behind absl/boost on raw speed generally

Keys with a weak, low-entropy, or attacker-influenced hash function: a bucket's collision chain is capped at ~2,048 keys, and hitting that repeatedly makes the table grow until it exhausts memory instead of degrading to a linear scan
Targeting an FPU-less embedded platform: the default max-load-factor check uses floating point (open issue #23 asks for an integer-only option)
Need active upstream maintenance guarantees: last commit 2025-05-06, tagged 'stale' by the catalog

integration.dependencies: none (C standard library only; malloc/free by default, both overridable)
integration.min_toolchain: C99 (with explicit HASH_FN/CMPR_FN); full vt_*-generic macro API requires C11 _Generic; tested under GCC, Clang, MinGW, and MSVC; usable from C++ via extern "C"
integration.platforms: not documented as architecture-restricted (portable C, no SIMD intrinsics in the header); an open issue notes the floating-point load-factor check is awkward on FPU-less embedded hardware
integration.thread_safety: not documented (no locking or concurrency support mentioned; treat as single-writer/no built-in synchronization)
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — different API shape (vt_insert/vt_get/vt_erase or NAME_-prefixed functions, iterator struct accessed as itr.data->key/->val), no operator[], manual NAME_cleanup required instead of RAII/destructor-driven free

gotchas: Insert, get_or_insert, erase, erase_itr, reserve, and shrink invalidate all existing iterators; use erase_itr's return value to keep iterating while deleting
No RAII: forgetting to call NAME_cleanup leaks the table's memory (a reported 'stuck insert' bug turned out to be missing cleanup across repeated runs, per issue #22)

A degenerate hash function (near-constant output) can make a bucket chain exceed its ~2,048-key limit, causing the table to keep doubling until allocation fails rather than falling back to a slow linear scan
Custom allocators need CTX_TY plus matching MALLOC_FN/FREE_FN signatures that take a size and context pointer, not a drop-in std::allocator interface
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Verstable when the code is C (or C++ that can bind to a C ABI) and you want a single-header, type-safe table with tombstone-free deletion and strong lookup/iteration speed; the sibling C++-only tables (ska::flat_hash_map/bytell_hash_map, tsl::robin_map, tsl::hopscotch_map) use similar open-addressing ideas but require a C++ compiler, and emhash/emilib2/google::dense_hash_map generally edge it out on raw insertion or peak throughput if a C-only API isn't a requirement.
verified_claims_summary: On the author's own interactive benchmark (GCC 13.2.0 via MinGW-w64, -O3 -DNDEBUG, AMD Ryzen 7 5800H at 90% locked frequency, libstdc++'s std::unordered_map as baseline, across 32-bit int, 64-bit-int/large-value, and string-key workloads), the page states std::unordered_map is far slower than most open-addressing tables except at looking up existing keys, and at least an order of magnitude slower at iteration; Verstable is described as having extremely fast lookups and erasures of nonexisting keys, iteration beaten only by boost::unordered_flat_map, emilib2, and contiguous-storage tables (and faster than absl::flat_hash_map on iteration), but 'only average' insertion speed. Results are shown as interactive charts rather than a numeric table.
status_note: Maintenance status is 'stale' (last commit 2025-05-06), but it's MIT-licensed and a single vendorable header, so freezing at the current commit carries little risk; the bigger adoption cost is its non-STL API rather than staleness.
